newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - NAM sees return to profits.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - NAM sees return to profits.

text.p: NAM Corp expects to return to profitability in fiscal 1998, the company's top executives said Wednesday.

In an interview, chief financial officer Pat Giuliani-Rheaume said expansion costs were the main reason the dispute arbitration services company posted a loss through the first nine months of its current fiscal year.
With many of those costs behind it, NAM expects "the fruit of its (expansion) investments to be a return to profitability in fiscal 1998," Giuliani-Rheaume said.

NAM is the only publicly-traded dispute resolution company, having launched an initial public offering last November. The company competes with the not-for-profit American Arbitration Association and the for-profit Judicial Arbitration Mediation Services Inc/Endispute.

It counts among its main clients corporations and municipalities such as NYNEX Corp, Conrail Inc and the cities of New York and Philadelphia. Law and insurance firms are significant markets for the company.
NAM's recent expansion efforts included new staff hiring and office openings as well as a new advertising campaign.

Over the first nine months of fiscal 1997, NAM posted a net loss of $237,000 on revenues of $2.5 million. A year ago, it earned $119,000 on $2.2 million in revenues through its first three quarters. NAM's fiscal year ends June 30.
Expectations are for revenue growth of 50 percent in the coming year, far outstripping its fiscal 1997 pace, NAM chief executive Roy Israel said.
"We're going to be back on track," he said.

Israel said the company is considering expanding its geographic coverage, eyeing office openings in Florida, northern New York, Arizona and North Carolina. It presently has offices in southern New York, South Carolina, Tennessee, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.
Israel said he was confident in the company's ability to expand its client base.

He pointed to NAM's customer retention rate as a key factor. "Over 50 percent of our clients are obtained by word-of-mouth," he said, noting 84 percent of NAM clients with two or more cases in 1995 returned again as customers in 1996.

To maintain and enhance growth, Israel said, NAM is considering entering the labor dispute settlement business. Early plans include a series of seminars on the benefits of alternative resolution methods in employment disputes such as unfair termination and sexual discrimination.
